title: CAPSUL: A Comprehensive Human Protein Benchmark for Subcellular Localization
claim: Our dataset is built by a three-step pipeline that merges structural data and curated annotations into one unified per-item record.
layout: 3 stages, snake-like flow: top row, bottom row, then right column; arrows connect
description: A flow diagram on three rounded pale-green panels. Step 1 (top left) takes proteins from the AlphaFold2 and UniProt databases. It shows thumbnails of green 3D protein structures, marks fragmented predictions with red X and green check icons, and keeps the unfragmented ones. It then extracts three outputs: an amino acid sequence string, a scatter plot of Cα coordinates, and a string of 3Di tokens. Step 2 (bottom left) combines UniProt and HPA annotations. Raw label text becomes small binary tables of nucleus, Golgi apparatus and mitochondria. These tables are merged by a union into a final table, and sticky-note icons name the locations. Step 3 (right) is a tall table giving one example protein record with ID, labels, split, sequence, length, tokens and coordinates. Thick light-blue arrows link the steps, and yellow database tags mark the sources.
caption: Procedures of CAPSUL dataset construction, including 3 key steps: Step 1 extracts and filters the sequence and structure data for each high-quality protein from AlphaFold2; Step 2 collects the annotations from UniProt and HPA for the resulting proteins in Step 1; Step 3 merges the structure data and the annotations for each protein, which consists of protein ID, localization annotations, amino acid sequence, sequence length, 3Di tokens, and C$\alpha$ coordinates, \etc
abstract: Subcellular localization is a crucial biological task for drug target identification and function annotation. Although it has been biologically realized that subcellular localization is closely associated with protein structure, no existing dataset offers comprehensive 3D structural information with detailed subcellular localization annotations, thus severely hindering the application of promising structure-based models on this task. To address this gap, we introduce a new benchmark called $\mathbf{CAPSUL}$, a $\mathbf{C}$omprehensive hum$\mathbf{A}$n $\mathbf{P}$rotein benchmark for $\mathbf{SU}$bcellular $\mathbf{L}$ocalization. It features a dataset that integrates diverse 3D structural representations with fine-grained subcellular localization annotations carefully curated by domain experts. We evaluate this benchmark using a variety of state-of-the-art sequence-based and structure-based models, showcasing the importance of involving structural features in this task. Furthermore, we explore reweighting and single-label classification strategies to facilitate future investigation on structure-based methods for this task. Lastly, we showcase the powerful interpretability of structure-based methods through a case study on the Golgi apparatus, where we discover a decisive localization pattern $Î±$-helix from attention mechanisms, demonstrating the potential for bridging the gap with intuitive biological interpretability and paving the way for data-driven discoveries in cell biology.
